system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

**What the study proposes.** Thornbury would roll out a single, uniform weekly food waste service to all 52,000 households from April 2027. The case rests on a six-month pilot covering 4,000 households, and on a net cost of about £490,000 a year, fully covered by a provisional £520,000 government ("new burdens") allocation.

The pilot design is strong. It mixed housing types, measured participation weekly by housing type, and its flat/house split matches the district's at 20% flats. The arithmetic in Table 2 also checks out:
- **Vehicles:** £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400.
- **Crews:** 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000.
- **Total:** £733,400.

The problem is that the study's own pilot data contradict its two main conclusions. Participation was *not* similar across housing types, and once that is corrected, the service is not fully funded.

## 1. Participation in flats was much lower

Table 1 shows 66% participation in houses and **21% in flats**. Flat-dwellers were about a third as likely to take part, and those who did produced less food waste (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg a week). Section 2 nonetheless calls participation "broadly similar," and the recommendation for a uniform service rests on that claim.

Flats usually need a different approach, such as communal bins, bin-store access and extra communications. The statutory requirement covers flats too. The pilot evidence points towards a separate flats approach, not away from it.

## 2. The tonnage projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies a "64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%** (2,280 ÷ 4,000). Since the pilot's housing mix matches the district's, 57% is the right figure. Projecting by housing type gives the same answer:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **2,870 tonnes**, not 3,290. The projection is overstated by about 13%.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected 2,870 tonnes leaves about 1,070 tonnes a year with nowhere local to go. On the study's own 3,290 tonnes, the shortfall is about 1,490 tonnes.

The surplus would have to go to the next plant, 46 miles away. Its gate fee is unknown, and the extra haulage cost is not included anywhere. "Treatment is local" holds for only part of the waste.

## 4. The disposal saving is too high

At £74 a tonne:

| Basis | Saving |
|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t) | £243,000 |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t), all at Brookfield's rate | ~£212,500 |
| Only 1,800 t at Brookfield's rate | £133,200, plus a smaller, unknown saving on the remaining ~1,070 t |

Even on the corrected tonnage with everything at Brookfield's rate, the net cost is £733,400 − £212,500 ≈ **£521,000**. That already slightly exceeds the £520,000 allocation, before the capacity problem and before the missing cost lines in the next section.

## 5. Cost lines that are missing

The cover note says "every cost line is shown." Table 2 leaves out:
- **Capital financing:** about £990,000 for vehicles is needed up front in December 2026. Depreciation spreads the cost across years, but not the interest or the timing of the outlay.
- **Haulage and gate fees** for tonnage beyond Brookfield's capacity.
- **Resilience:** a spare vehicle, and agency cover for crew sickness and holidays. Six crews with no spare is fragile for a weekly statutory service.
- **Supervision and management**, plus any depot changes.
- **One-off launch costs:** the dedicated phone line and web page, recruitment, training, delivering caddies to 52,000 households, and the March leaflet.
- **Liners after the first three months**, if they are supplied on an ongoing basis.

## 6. Funding and timing risks

- **The allocation is provisional.** The Council would commit £990,000 to vehicles in December 2026 against funding that isn't confirmed.
- **Brookfield has offered capacity but not signed a contract.** Secure the contract before ordering vehicles.
- **The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles arrive in March, crews are trained in March, and collections start on 5 April. A late vehicle delivery delays the launch.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Seasonality and novelty.** The pilot ran January to June, so summer volumes and early enthusiasm may not reflect a full year.
- **The satisfaction survey.** "81% of surveyed households" needs a response rate. If mostly participating households replied, the figure is flattering.
- **Contamination.** The under-2% contamination figure, and the steady fall in missed collections, are genuinely good results and worth keeping.

## How the cover note differs from the document

- "Participation held up across houses and flats" is contradicted by Table 1: 66% against 21%.
- "Consistent yields" overlooks the 1.9 kg and 1.4 kg difference.
- "Every cost line is shown" is not the case; see section 5.
- "Fully covered" fails once the participation rate is corrected.
- "Treatment is local" holds only up to 1,800 tonnes.

## What to fix before Cabinet

1. Use 57% participation, or project by housing type, giving about 2,870 tonnes.
2. Drop the claim of similar participation, and propose a flats approach with its own costs.
3. Model treatment beyond Brookfield's 1,800 tonnes: the far plant's gate fee plus haulage, until 2029.
4. Add the missing cost lines and show capital financing separately.
5. Restate the net cost against the provisional £520,000, with a sensitivity range, and state what happens if the allocation comes in lower.
6. Secure the Brookfield contract and confirmed funding before the vehicle order, or present the order as a decision taken at risk.

The service is statutory, so the question isn't whether to proceed but on what basis. The pilot gives the Council strong local evidence. Read correctly, that evidence shows a service needing a flats strategy, constrained by treatment capacity until 2029, and costing somewhat more than the expected funding. Cabinet should approve the roll-out on that basis.
